name: Mixture Model (e.g., GMM, DPM)
analogy: Think of it as sorting a pile of 5-minute bars into a few bins by feel, except no bar is forced into one bin. Each bar gets a share in every bin, so a bar that is half quiet and half busy is allowed to say so.

steps.title: Decide how many kinds of bar there are
steps.description: You choose how many hidden groups might have produced the data. A Gaussian mixture needs this number chosen up front, usually by comparing fits; the Dirichlet process version lets the data suggest how many groups it needs.
steps.inExample: Three groups are chosen for MNQ 5-minute bars: a quiet group, a normal group and a fast group.

steps.title: Give each group a rough starting shape
steps.description: Every group starts with a guessed center, a guessed spread and a guessed share of all bars. These guesses can be poor, because the next steps repair them.
steps.inExample: The quiet group starts centered on a 10-point average true range, the fast group on 35 points, and each group starts with a third of the bars.

steps.title: Give every bar a share in every group
steps.description: For each bar, the model asks how likely each group was to have produced a bar that looks like this. The answers become shares that add to 100 percent, so a borderline bar is split instead of being forced into one group.
steps.inExample: In the first round, a bar with a 6-bar gain of 24 points and a 21-point range is split 20 percent quiet, 55 percent normal and 25 percent fast.

steps.title: Move each group toward the bars it owns
steps.description: Each group's center, spread and overall share are recomputed using the bars weighted by their shares. A group is pulled mostly toward the bars that belong to it most.
steps.inExample: The normal group's center shifts to an 18-point average true range and its share of all bars rises from a third to about 38 percent.

steps.title: Repeat until the groups stop moving
steps.description: The share-giving step and the moving step alternate. Each round fits the data at least a little better, until the changes are too small to matter. The result is a local best fit, so different starting guesses can land on different answers.
steps.inExample: After about 40 rounds the three groups hold steady: quiet near 45 percent of bars, normal near 40 percent, fast near 15 percent.

steps.title: Place a new bar among the groups
steps.description: A new bar is run through the share-giving step once more using the finished groups. The output is its share in each group, and also how typical it is of the whole mixture.
steps.inExample: The new 14:35 bar comes out 18 percent quiet, 57 percent normal and 25 percent fast.

useFor.example: Sorting MNQ 5-minute bars into quiet, normal and fast groups from average true range and volume, so position size can scale with how fast the market is.
Flagging a bar whose range and volume fit none of the three groups well, as a candidate data error or a genuine tail event.
Feeding the three group shares into a gradient boosting model as extra columns beside the 35 base features.
Letting overnight, London and New York behavior fall into different groups from combined intraday ES data.

avoidWhen: The order of the bars matters, because this model treats every bar as independent; a hidden Markov model keeps track of which group the market was in a moment ago.
You need a prediction of direction, because a mixture only describes what kinds of bars exist, not what happens after them.

example.scenario: A mixture of three groups was fit on twelve months of MNQ 5-minute bars. The 14:35 bar has just closed and you want to know which kind of bar it is.

input.summary: A few features of the bar that just closed, the same columns used when the three groups were fit.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, a measure of how fast the market is moving.

fields.name: range of this bar
fields.meaning: The distance from this bar's low to its high; one point is worth 2 US dollars per contract.

fields.name: gain over the last 6 bars
fields.meaning: How far price has risen over the previous 30 minutes.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

output.summary: A share of belonging for each of the three groups, plus how ordinary the bar is.

fields.name: share in the quiet group
fields.meaning: The probability that this bar came from the quiet kind of market.

fields.name: share in the normal group
fields.meaning: The probability that this bar came from the normal kind of market.

fields.name: share in the fast group
fields.meaning: The probability that this bar came from the fast kind of market.

fields.name: how typical the bar is
fields.value: typical, not among the rarest 5 percent
fields.meaning: Whether the bar fits the fitted mixture well or looks like an outlier.

example.reading: The bar leans normal but carries a real quarter share of the fast group, so volatility may be rising. A sensible use is to size positions with the blended picture, for example a weighted average of each group's usual stop distance, instead of acting on the single most likely group.
